paras: The Racquet Club arrests took place in New York on the night of June 8, 1882, when a policeman entered the Racquet Club on Sixth Avenue to arrest John Whitehurst, a Black waiter accused of taking a purse, without a warrant. After two of the men he was serving objected, police reinforcements took the waiter and the club men to the station house, and Whitehurst later testified that the arresting officer struck him twice. The papers treated it mainly as a dispute over the club men's rights, and in July a police justice ruled the arrest lawful.

According to a New York Times report reprinted in Richmond, John Carson (spelled Carlson) missed a purse he said held $3 in Rushton's drug store, on the ground floor of the club building, and was told that a colored servant of the club had left with a purse in his hand. Carson went to the Twenty-ninth Precinct station house, and Policeman Frederick Ringler was sent to arrest the waiter.

Ringler found Whitehurst serving club member Jose Aymar and the lawyer Thomas C. Bach at dinner. By Whitehurst's account, he offered to go once he had seen his employers, but they would not let him go, and Ringler then gave him "two severe blows, one on the arm and one on the shoulder." Bach testified that he questioned the warrantless arrest and offered to let Captain Alexander S. Williams decide; Ringler said Aymar and Bach barred the door against him and his prisoner.

After Ringler called from a window to Carson, who alerted Captain Williams, the size of the squad that followed was reported as a roundsman and four patrolmen by the Sun, eighteen policemen by the Times, and "at least fourteen" by the club men. The officers forced the door, and Aymar, still in a dressing gown, was taken through the street to the station with Bach and the waiter. A club member testified that an officer struck at Aymar with his club from behind in the hall, and a doctor found two bruises on Aymar's shoulder and arm the next day.

The next morning Justice Ford discharged Whitehurst, "there not being the slightest evidence" against him, and fined Aymar and Bach $10 each for interfering with an officer. Charles E. Jenkins, a club member, wrote asking Carson not to press the charge and offered to cover any loss, and Carson withdrew it.

In July Aymar and Bach charged Policemen Ringler, Lehne, Weeks and Phelps with trespass, assault and battery and false arrest before Justice Smith at the Jefferson Market Police Court. At the hearings Whitehurst repeated that he had been struck, Bach thought he saw a club fall on the waiter's arm, and the officers denied any clubbing. On July 19 Justice Smith ruled that the arrest of Whitehurst was lawful and the complainants' action illegal, dismissed the case and discharged the policemen.
In August Whitehurst was arrested again, this time on a janitor's charge that he had drawn a knife, and papers identified him as the waiter at the center of the June affair.

The New-York Tribune first mocked the "hilarious young gentlemen" as "practical jokers" who had locked up a policeman, but by July it ran the hearings under the headline "Charges of Police Brutality." The Sun devoted a front-page editorial to the law of arrest, concluding that the attempt to take "the negro servant" without a warrant was "clearly" unlawful and that the fines on the club men were wrong.

A Washington Evening Star letter said the club had won "renown by fighting policemen" and that opinion favored the police, while the Richmond Dispatch reprinted the Times and Herald accounts. A syndicated New York letter carried in Vermont and Michigan on June 23 treated the affair as comedy at the expense of "gilded youth" and called the waiter "the darkey."

The Times report said younger members locked the door "in a spirit of mischief," and the janitor heard a member remark that they had a policeman locked in, but Aymar and Bach swore the door was never locked. On the clubbing, Whitehurst, Aymar and a club witness described blows, and Ringler, Lehne and the roundsman said they saw none.

bases: Twenty-ninth Precinct policemen arrested a Black waiter without a warrant, and he testified the arresting officer struck him twice (A2, A14).
Many reports agree on the warrantless arrest and the police entry into the club (A2, A3, A14), but the officers denied the clubbing that Whitehurst and the club men described (A14, A15).

accounts.label: Policeman's version
accounts.gist: Ringler said Aymar and Bach barred the door and locked him in with his prisoner, so he called from the window for help; the officers denied any clubbing.

accounts.label: Club men's version
accounts.gist: Aymar and Bach said the door was never locked, that they only questioned an arrest without a warrant, and that officers clubbed Aymar and dragged him out half-dressed.

accounts.label: Waiter's testimony
accounts.gist: Whitehurst said he offered to go once he had seen his employers, that they refused to let him go, and that Ringler gave him two blows on the arm and shoulder.

accounts.label: New York Times report
accounts.gist: Younger members locked the door 'in a spirit of mischief' while laughing over the arrest; eighteen policemen came and took the waiter and three men.

framing.detail: The Sun's editorial held the warrantless arrest of 'the negro servant' 'clearly' unlawful and the fines on the club men wrong, without discussing force.
The Tribune first mocked the 'hilarious young gentlemen' as 'practical jokers', then headed its July report 'Charges of Police Brutality'.
The Evening Star letter called the truth 'in some doubt' and said opinion favored the police; its later piece set both versions side by side.
A syndicated New York letter treated the affair as comedy at the expense of 'gilded youth', calling the waiter 'the darkey'.
The Richmond Dispatch reprinted New York Times and Herald reports under 'A Racket in the Racket Club' and 'Justice Smith supports the police'.
